meta.title: Environmental politics knowledge network, c. 1968-2026
meta.description: Key works and debates in environmental and climate politics: the international climate regime, transnational and private governance, governance architecture and earth system governance, the political economy of climate policy, public opinion, denial and the countermovement, parties and populism, policy instruments, energy transitions, environmental and climate justice, adaptation, the commons, natural resources and the resource curse, climate and conflict, the environmental state and democracy, trade, finance and corporate power, and movements and litigation. Seeds come from this repo's papers.json; works shared with the other maps are imported from them; others are top-cited 2006-2026 articles selected via Crossref (nine environmental journals plus political science journals) and anchoring books and classics. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work).

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works come from the user's Zotero library. Works imported from the other maps keep their verification. Crossref-selected works take title, authors, year, venue and DOI from Crossref records. Anchors are checked in Crossref separately; see each node's `verified` field. One-line claims for non-repo works are my summaries.

edges.why: Epistemic communities enable cooperation on shared resources.
Paris and the logic of pledge and review.
Interests and norms in climate support.
Traces how vulnerable states framed loss and damage in UNFCCC talks, extending debates over justice in international adaptation finance.
Nonstate actors from Copenhagen to Paris.
New directions in earth system governance.
Places environmental authoritarianism within a typology of planetary sovereignty scenarios, from Climate Leviathan to Climate Mao.
Utility retrenchment of clean energy laws.
Green industrial policy transforms climate politics.
Reviews global survey evidence on public support for the sustainable development values set out in the Brundtland report.
Ideology and climate views in the EU.
Environmentalism of the poor in the Global South.
Indigenous climate justice and tipping points.
Property rights and the resource curse.
Economic adaptation through investment and migration.
Race to the bottom among states.
Water brings cooperation more than war.
No resource curse in long-run data.
What we know about the resource curse.
Democracy works only with low corruption.
Applies the ecological modernization discourse to China's shifting environmental governance.
Like Ponte, shows how corporate claims of greening global supply chains hide environmental costs, here for artificial intelligence.
Extends Stokes's retrospective backlash against wind siting to a costly vehicle regulation and to gains for a radical-right party.
Gives causal evidence for Lockwood's claim that right-wing populists profit from the costs climate policies impose on aggrieved groups.
Shows that compensating coal regions with a just transition deal can reverse the incumbent punishment Stokes documented.
Tests in real elections the survey finding that compensating vulnerable workers builds support for climate policy.
Specifies the populism-climate link by showing the radical right uses climate opposition as a wedge against the mainstream right.
Applies niche-party issue competition to climate, showing radical-right positioning pressures mainstream parties.
Finds disasters raise Green vote shares in Germany, showing that in multiparty systems a dedicated green party captures the experience effect that wildfires produced in US ballot voting.
Carries the finding that local weather experiences shape climate attitudes through to actual party choice.
Builds on evidence that mainstream left parties' environmental positioning decides whether green attitudes flow to new Green parties.
Re-tests across 33 countries Inglehart's claim that environmental concern rises with affluence and postmaterialist values.
Shows national vulnerability to climate impacts, alongside affluence, shapes concern, qualifying the postmaterialist account of environmental support.
Extends the local-weather finding to long-run state temperature trends, showing warming raises public concern.
Integrates the authors' weather-experience evidence into a review of the partisan and experiential sources of US climate opinion.
Documents the partisan polarization of US climate beliefs from 2001 to 2010 that the conservative think-tank denial campaign sought to produce.
Generalizes the conservative-white-male finding to decade-long partisan and ideological polarization of the whole public.
Builds on the documented partisan divide to show elite cues, not scientific literacy, drive Republican doubt about climate change.
Shows voters reward executives who respond to disasters with declarations and aid, refining Healy and Malhotra's account of myopic disaster voting.
Uses evidence that voters reward relief but not preparedness to argue political incentives discourage proactive climate adaptation.
Argues social networks, more than physical or financial resources, determine recovery, adding social capital to the components of adaptive capacity.
Draws on political-science evidence about social capital and disaster recovery to argue adaptation is a core political problem.
Argues activists govern by reshaping social and economic practices directly, contesting regime accounts that run environmental influence through states and expert networks.
Extends Wapner's world civic politics to campaigns that hold corporations accountable for their climate impacts.
Builds its review of climate litigation on Vanhala's account of how legal opportunity structures shape NGOs' turn to courts.
Shows NGOs' choice of litigation versus other tactics depends on national legal opportunity structures, a domestic-institutional complement to Hadden's network account of tactics.
Treats the Acre rubber tappers as a paradigm case of livelihood-based environmentalism of the poor.
Carries the linkage of social equity and environmental protection from US environmental justice to forest-dependent workers in the Brazilian Amazon.
Tests Ostrom's account of self-organized collective action on US watersheds, finding partnerships emerge where benefits are high and organizing costs low.
Builds on the watershed-partnership findings to model collaborative institutions as an ecology of interacting games.
Shows democratization accelerates deforestation through electoral incentives, contesting the view that democracy reduces environmental degradation.
Adds an electoral-cycle mechanism to evidence that democracy's environmental benefits are conditional.
Identifies campaign donations as a second political channel, beside electoral incentives, through which local politics drives deforestation.
Shows organized economic interests buy weaker environmental policy, here via campaign finance and lax enforcement in Brazil rather than US state legislatures.
Argues Hardin's commons metaphor has been misapplied to non-commons problems such as climate, distorting policy design.
Joins Aklin and Mildenberger in rejecting the collective-action framing of climate in favor of problem-specific diagnoses.
Extends the epistemic-community argument from Mediterranean pollution control to the ozone regime and the CFC ban.
Explains ozone policy by states' ecological vulnerability and abatement costs, contesting Haas's epistemic-community account.
Revives the interest-based approach, locating climate politics' central obstacle in domestic distributive conflict over abatement costs.
Emphasizes self-enforcement and the strategic limits of treaty participation, against Young's view that institutional bargaining under uncertainty readily produces regimes.
Argues states sharing resources can form regimes through institutional bargaining, qualifying Hardin's expectation that commons end in tragedy without coercion.
Explains the spread of environmental treaties and ministries by world-society scientific culture rather than functional problem-solving by expert networks.
Builds on world-society arguments by testing transnational communication as a driver of environmental policy convergence.
Argues climate clubs face participation and expansion hurdles that make them an uncertain route to broad cooperation, tempering Nordhaus's proposal.
Develops the minilateral club logic Falkner assessed, specifying conditions under which clubs could grow.
Extends coalitional accounts of climate policy to international bargaining, showing polluting trade-exposed sectors shape negotiation positions.
Uses evidence that industrial interests drive negotiation positions to support a distributive-conflict view of climate politics.
Formalizes why some firms back climate regulation, to raise rivals' costs, explaining the business coalitions Meckling traced around emissions trading.
Builds on firm-level competitive logics of regulatory support in classifying firms as transitioning, hedging or resisting decarbonization.
Empirically tests whether the proliferating, loosely coupled climate regime complex undermines or sustains states' cooperative effort.
Puts to a cross-national test the claim that fragmented governance architectures weaken cooperation.
Links petro-state politics to energy pricing, showing oil-producing and low-capacity states subsidize rather than tax fossil fuels.
Adds the politics of fossil-fuel subsidies, in effect a negative carbon price, to explanations of why pricing carbon is hard.
Experimentally isolates political trust as a cause of opposition to environmental taxes, a determinant highlighted in reviews of policy support.
Draws on evidence that distrust of government drives opposition to carbon taxes in recommending earmarking and revenue recycling.
Refines sector-specific political logics by showing climate policy depends on coalitions with firms that can profitably decarbonize.
Frames decarbonization as a bargain among asset holders who gain and lose, in line with the asset-revaluation view.
Develops a typology of the green industrial policy strategies by which states position firms in clean-tech supply chains.
Tests whether non-state, market-driven programs change behavior, finding ISO 14001 members improve regulatory compliance.
Builds on green-club theory to show ISO 14001 spreads through trade ties instead of a race to the bottom.
Updates Trading Up by showing the EU overtook the US as the more stringent environmental and consumer regulator.
Extends the transatlantic regulatory reversal to explain the EU and US switching roles in international environmental treaties.
Builds on cross-national evidence of democracies' stronger environmental commitment, separating climate commitments from actual effort.
Qualifies the democracy-environment link by showing democracies cut emissions only where corruption is low.
Organizes cognitive, societal and statist explanations of the resource curse, including Karl's account of petro-state institutional decay.
Moves from reviewing political explanations of the resource curse to a cross-national test of oil's anti-democratic effect.
Argues oil is endogenous to prior industrialization and, once modeled, does not hinder democracy, challenging Ross's central finding.
Joins Haber and Menaldo's revisionist challenge to the political resource curse with an endogeneity argument.
Expands the 1994 case evidence into a general theory of resource capture, ecological marginalization and violence.
Faults scarcity-conflict case research for selecting on the dependent variable and omitting political and economic variables.
Answers Gleditsch's call for systematic tests, finding little support for drought-driven conflict.
Argues environmental stress turns violent only through weak institutions and state capacity, challenging deterministic scarcity-conflict claims.
Supports Salehyan's skepticism by finding climate variability does not robustly predict African civil wars once political factors are modeled.
Shows conflict degrades weather-station records, so temperature measures used to link warming to civil war are not exogenous.
Implies meta-analytic climate-conflict estimates may be biased by conflict-induced measurement error in climate data.
Expert elicitation reconciles strong climate-conflict estimates with skeptics, judging climate a real but secondary conflict driver.
Incorporates skeptical findings like Buhaug's by ranking climate below development and state capacity as conflict risks.
Develops their urban climate research into an account of how the CCP network governs transnationally by bypassing national states.
Tests whether membership in transnational municipal networks like CCP spreads local climate policies.
Develops the 2004 diagnosis of global, intergenerational and theoretical 'storms' into a book-length argument.
Builds on Gardiner's mapping of climate ethics to argue the advantaged bear mitigation duties beyond their causal contribution.
Argues resource rents can promote democracy in unequal societies by easing elites' fear of redistribution, challenging Ross's oil-impedes-democracy thesis.
Re-examines the Syrian case and finds no sound evidence that climate-driven drought contributed to the civil war.
Explains oil's anti-democratic effect by how oil production weakened labor's power to disrupt, rather than by rentier fiscal mechanisms.
Shares Mitchell's materialist account of how energy regimes shape power, tracing coal-fired steam to capital's control over labor.
Applies the regime-complex framework to global energy governance, showing it evolved through punctuated equilibrium.
